summary: Torrance sits on 24.6 square miles of gently sloping coastal plain in the South Bay, and yet it functions less like a bedroom community and more like a self-contained employment hub — Honda's North American headquarters, a major Del Amo Fashion Center retail complex, and a dense corridor of aerospace and defense contractors along the 405 freeway mean a significant share of jobs exist within the city itself, a rarity for an LA-area suburb of 143,000. The climate is almost monotonously pleasant: an average daytime high of 73°F year-round with 9.2 hours of sunshine daily, cooled by marine-layer mornings that burn off by midday. A median home value just above $1.03 million against a median household income of $113,000 puts the price-to-income ratio above nine — steep even by Southern California standards, meaning a median-income household carrying that mortgage would be stretched well past conventional lending guidelines. Rent at $2,214 a month is more digestible but still claims roughly a quarter of that median pre-tax income. The 1.5-mile stretch of Torrance Beach connects to the Marvin Braude Bike Trail running along the coast, and the city maintains over 30 parks, giving it genuine walkable green space rather than just landscaped medians. Del Amo Fashion Center — one of the largest enclosed malls in the country — anchors a retail and dining cluster that ranges from ramen counters to sit-down seafood, lending the city a commercial gravity that most suburbs its size simply lack. Torrance is the rare LA-area city where you could theoretically work, shop, dine, and reach the ocean without ever touching a freeway — but affording to own there increasingly requires income well above the local median.
